Codex Worktrees and Session Forks

Use codex fork SESSION_ID to start a new conversation from a saved session. Add --worktree when you also want a separate Git checkout. Confirm the new conversation ID and the checkout path before editing. Check for uncommitted files first. In our CLI test, the managed worktree started at the same commit and left those changes in the original directory.

  1. Choose a fork, worktree or resume
  2. Fork the conversation
  3. Create a separate checkout
  4. Continue the current conversation
  5. Compare the observed results

What needs its own copy?

See stepsSee stepsSee steps

Fork a conversation in the current checkout

From the project where you already work, pass the saved session ID. If Codex offers a folder choice, check the checkout before accepting it.

codex fork SESSION_ID

Use this when you want to explore a second approach while preserving the first conversation. A regular fork can still share the same directory with the original session. If both sessions will edit files, choose a separate worktree.

For a non-interactive fork, save JSON events if you need to verify the new ID. With a prompt, this command also starts a turn.

codex exec --json fork SESSION_ID "Outline an alternative without editing files." > fork.jsonl
jq -r 'select(.type == "thread.started") | .thread_id' fork.jsonl

Fork into a separate Git worktree

  1. Run git status --short in the source checkout. If the fork depends on uncommitted work, save it in the intended starting commit or make a deliberate plan to carry over the specific files.
  2. Use a local Codex CLI and the explicit saved session ID. Check codex fork --help for availability on your installed version.
  3. Confirm the new directory with git worktree list. Run git status --short and git rev-parse HEAD in the new checkout before asking Codex to edit. Make sure required local setup is present.
codex fork SESSION_ID --worktree

For a non-interactive test from the same saved session:

codex exec --json fork --worktree SESSION_ID "Outline an alternative without editing files." > worktree-fork.jsonl

To start without saved conversation history, launch a new codex --worktree session. For the desktop app’s separate setup and handoff controls, see the official worktrees guide.

Continue the same conversation

If you're continuing the same approach, resume the saved session and confirm the ID. Use the Codex resume guide for the picker, --last and working-directory checks. If you are unsure where the session will edit, verify the path before sending a task that changes files.

What changed in our Codex CLI test

We ran Codex CLI 0.172.0 on macOS in a disposable Git repo. Both non-interactive forks gave a fresh thread ID and included the synthetic parent prompt in their loopback request. The saved parent session file stayed byte-for-byte the same.

One saved conversation, two forks
CommandConversationWorking directory
exec forkNew ID, inherited promptOriginal checkout
exec fork --worktreeNew ID, inherited promptSeparate checkout, same starting commit

The new checkout opened in detached HEAD and did not contain the parent’s uncommitted tracked edit or its untracked file. After we edited the tracked file directly in the new checkout, the original file still held the original edit. A Git worktree gives each session a working directory. File access still depends on Codex’s sandbox and permissions.

Download the fork IDs, Git checks and before-and-after file contents. The local fixture returned fixed text. We tested the non-interactive CLI, and the interactive commands above are documented. See the official CLI reference.
